draft.title: How Mumbai University uses your personal data: privacy notice
draft.summary: Mumbai University is a university that admits students, runs examinations and teaching, and keeps in touch with its students, alumni and event guests. This notice explains each purpose we ask your consent for, what it gives you, and the personal data it needs. You can agree to each purpose separately. Where a student is under eighteen, we ask a parent or lawful guardian to give consent for them.

purposes.title: Admissions
purposes.uses: We use this to check whether you are eligible for a course, verify your documents and keep you informed about your application. If the applicant is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent first.
dataItems: Category certificate, where you apply under a category

purposes.title: Examinations and results
purposes.uses: We use this to register you for examinations, conduct them, publish your results and handle any revaluation you ask for.

purposes.title: Your student record
purposes.uses: We use this to run your time at the University, from enrolment to completion, including attendance, fees and the documents you submit. If the student is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent first.

purposes.title: Online learning
purposes.uses: We use this to give you access to online courses, receive your assignments, record your grades and track your academic progress.
dataItems: Activity logs on the learning platform

purposes.title: Scholarships and fee concessions
purposes.uses: We use this to check whether you are eligible for a scholarship or concession and to pay it to you.

purposes.title: Sharing with your affiliated college
purposes.uses: We use this to exchange your academic and examination records with your affiliated college so that your studies and examinations can be administered.
dataItems: Submissions made by your college about you

purposes.title: Student help chatbot
purposes.uses: We use this to answer your questions through an automated chat assistant and to improve the help we give.
dataItems: Contact details, only if you choose to give them

purposes.title: Events and webinars
purposes.uses: We use this to register you for University events and webinars and to send you information about them.

purposes.title: Photographs at University events
purposes.uses: We use this to take photographs and video recordings at University events and share them to report on the event.

purposes.title: Alumni updates
purposes.uses: We use this to keep in touch after you graduate: news, alumni events, and invitations to support the University by donating.

law.point: A request for consent must come with, or after, a notice describing the personal data and the purpose it is used for.
The notice must stand on its own, use clear and plain language, itemise the personal data and describe each specified purpose and what it provides. This Rule applies from 13 May 2027.
Consent must be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, and limited to the data needed for each purpose. That is why each purpose is listed separately.
Before processing a child's personal data (a child is anyone under eighteen), the University must obtain verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian.
The University must take reasonable steps to check that the person consenting as parent is an identifiable adult.
Some processing can rely on 'certain legitimate uses' instead of consent, for example legal duties or employment. Such purposes should not appear in a consent notice.
People must be offered the notice in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.
The consent request must be in clear and plain language and give contact details for a person who can respond about rights.

missingInformation: The lawful basis for all nine records is not yet decided. Counsel should confirm which purposes truly need consent; any that rest on a legal duty or a State function under s.7 should be removed from this notice.

Examinations, student records, affiliated-college sharing and scholarships may fall under s.7 (for example legal or regulatory duties). Counsel to confirm before they are presented as optional consents.

Faculty data appears in the online learning and affiliated-college records. Staff data may rest on the employment use under s.7(i), so counsel should confirm whether faculty belong in this notice at all.
The admissions and scholarship records involve parents' or guardians' own data, but the records do not list which parent details are collected. Please add them as itemised data.
Please confirm whether the student-record purpose genuinely involves students under eighteen, and how the University will verify the parent's consent under Rule 10.
Please confirm whether the chatbot uses an external AI vendor and whether chat logs are used to improve it, so the uses wording is accurate.
Please confirm whether alumni donation appeals should be a separate purpose from alumni news, so people can consent to each separately.
Translations into Eighth Schedule languages are not yet prepared and are needed before publication.

law.point: The University must give people the option to read its notice in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution. Marathi is one of these languages.
The notice must be understandable on its own, without needing any other document. The Marathi version should therefore read clearly by itself.

The notice must give, in clear and plain language, an itemised list of the personal data and the specified purpose (the purpose named in the notice) with what each use provides. Each purpose above keeps its own data items and uses.
A request for consent must also be in clear and plain language, with the option to read it in English or an Eighth Schedule language.
Rule 3 on notices comes into force eighteen months after publication of the Rules, that is from 13 May 2027.

missingInformation: A fluent Marathi reader should check the whole translation for accuracy, tone and plain wording before publication.
Confirm the University's official Marathi name; the record says 'Mumbai University' but the notice says 'University of Mumbai'.
Confirm the preferred Marathi term for 'alumni updates'; the draft uses 'माजी विद्यार्थ्यांसाठी माहिती' (information for alumni).
The introduction mentions withdrawing consent, rights and complaints; confirm that TrustStack prints the matching Marathi details beside it, as Rule 3(c) requires a link and means for these.
Check that the English and Marathi versions stay in step whenever the English notice changes.

answer.answer: A draft front-page narrative for the provisional DPDP Exposure Brief, version 1, for a person to check and edit before it is printed.

draft.headline: The brief is provisional: 123 questions are unanswered, all 4 applicable penalty heads remain at stake, and 203 days remain until 13 May 2027.
paragraphs: This brief reads Mumbai University's readiness as of 22 October 2026. Its basis is provisional, because the baseline assessment is still in progress and 123 questions are unanswered. The figures below will change as those answers come in. A reviewer decides whether any answer or evidence is accepted.

The statutory ceilings at stake total ₹700 crore across 4 of 4 applicable penalty heads. These are the maximums the Act allows, set by the Schedule under s.33(1). They are not a predicted fine. The Board (the Data Protection Board of India) decides any penalty, and only after an inquiry. Security safeguards (₹250 crore ceiling) and children and lawful guardians (₹200 crore ceiling) are not yet assessed, because no question that evidences them has been answered. Breach notification (₹200 crore ceiling) is partially mitigated, assessed from 1 personal data breach recorded in the breach register. The 'any other provision' head (₹50 crore ceiling) is exposed, because 2 processors have no contract with DPDP clauses recorded. Significant Data Fiduciary duties are not applicable, as no notification is recorded.

The brief also notes that the processing register's gaps have never been generated. The action table is empty, so no open action yet counts against a penalty head at stake. On pace, 3 critical and high items and 4 items in all are outstanding. The university is closing about 0 actions a week, against 0.2 a week needed to finish all work by 13 May 2027, when most of the DPDP Rules commence. There is not enough history yet to forecast a finish date.

The brief records one further point for awareness. Under s.37, after penalties in two or more instances, the Board may advise the Central Government to direct blocking of public access to a service. This is a statutory feature to keep in view, not a forecast.
bullets: Direct the assessment team to answer the 123 outstanding questions, so the provisional basis can be firmed up.
Ask for the processing register's gaps to be generated, as the brief notes this has never been done.
Record valid contracts with DPDP clauses for the 2 processors that have none, given s.8(2).
Ask for evidence on security safeguards and on children and lawful guardians, so these heads can be assessed.
Review the handling of the 1 recorded personal data breach against s.8(6) and Rule 7.
Ask why the action table is empty while 3 critical and high items are outstanding. Ensure each item has an owner and a due date.
Raise the closing pace from about 0 actions a week towards the 0.2 a week the brief says is needed before 13 May 2027.
Ask counsel to confirm the legal reading behind each head before any decision is taken.

law.point: The Board may impose a monetary penalty from the Schedule only after an inquiry finds a significant breach and the person has been heard. The ₹700 crore figure is a total of ceilings, not a prediction.
The university, as Data Fiduciary (the body that decides why and how personal data is used), stays responsible for processing done by it or by its processors.
A Data Processor (a vendor processing data on the university's behalf) may be engaged only under a valid contract. This is the reason the 'any other provision' head is shown as exposed.
The university must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach. This head is not yet assessed.
The Board and each affected person must be told of a personal data breach in the prescribed form and manner.
The Board is told of a breach without delay, with a detailed report within the period this rule sets.
After the Board imposes penalties in two or more instances, it may advise the Central Government to direct blocking of public access to a service.
Most of the Rules, including notice, security, breach, children and rights, commence eighteen months after publication, which the brief gives as 13 May 2027.

missingInformation: The action table is empty, so the bullets draw on the brief's notices and reasons, not on listed actions. A person should confirm which actions exist.
The answers to the 123 unanswered questions, which will change every head's status.
Whether the university processes children's personal data, which bears on the s.9 head. This is not yet assessed.
The facts of the 1 recorded breach and how it was notified. These are needed to read the breach notification head.
Which 2 processors lack DPDP contract clauses, and the current state of those contracts.
The indicative 'upper third' ranges are left out of the narrative, because TrustStack never predicts a penalty.
Owners and due dates for the 3 critical and high outstanding items.

answer.answer: A draft front-page narrative for the provisional Regulator-Ready Evidence Pack, version 1, for a person to check and edit before it is printed.

draft.headline: The assessment is still in progress, and evidence is thin across every penalty head that applies, so the priority is to gather and review evidence before 13 May 2027.
paragraphs: This pack is provisional. It is based on the assessment 'Mumbai University DPDP Compass Baseline', where 123 questions are still unanswered. It is dated 22 October 2026, which is 203 days before 13 May 2027, when most of the DPDP Rules commence. The figures will change as the assessment is completed. They are a readiness picture, not a legal opinion.

The report shows 4 of 4 applicable penalty heads at stake, with statutory ceilings of ₹700 crore. These are the maximums the Schedule to the Act allows. They are not a predicted fine, and the Board decides any penalty only after an inquiry. 'Any other provision' is shown as Exposed. Breach notification is Partially mitigated but has no artefacts behind it. Security safeguards and children's data are Not yet assessed. Significant Data Fiduciary duties are shown as Not applicable.

Four artefacts (stored documents or records offered as evidence) are held. A reviewer has rated one as Adequate and one as Partial, and two are awaiting review. Most obligation areas have no artefacts at all, including notice, consent, Data Principal rights, retention and breach readiness. None of the 10 live processing records has evidence attached. The processing register's gaps have never been generated.

No remediation action has been closed, and 4 remain outstanding. Evidence of mitigation, and how promptly it was taken, is a factor the Board weighs under s.33(2)(e). Building that record now matters.
bullets: Answer the 123 outstanding assessment questions so the baseline is no longer provisional.
Arrange review of the 2 artefacts awaiting review by someone other than the uploader; a reviewer decides whether to accept each one.
Generate the processing register's gaps, which have never been run.
Attach evidence to the 10 live processing records, none of which has any yet.
Gather evidence for personal data breach readiness, which is marked Partially mitigated with no artefacts.
Collect evidence for the 'any other provision' areas, including notice, consent, rights, grievance redressal and retention.
Complete the assessment of security safeguards and of children's data and guardian consent.
Progress the 4 outstanding remediation actions; a person closes each action on evidence or a reviewer's approval.

law.point: The University, as Data Fiduciary (the body that decides why and how personal data is used), is responsible for meeting the Act, including for processing done by its vendors.
The Board may impose a monetary penalty from the Schedule only after an inquiry finds a significant breach and the organisation has been heard.
When setting a penalty, the Board considers whether action was taken to mitigate a breach, and how timely and effective it was.
The Board may inquire into an organisation's affairs and inspect its documents and registers, which is the audience this pack is prepared for.
After penalties in two or more instances, the Board may advise the Central Government to direct blocking of public access.
The law sets a grievance response period not exceeding ninety days, which must be published; it sets no thirty-day deadline for rights requests.
TrustStack's own thirty-day target for answering rights requests sits inside the law's ceiling; it is TrustStack's target, not the law.

missingInformation: The request to say the law requires rights requests to be answered within 30 days was left out; that is TrustStack's target, not the law.
The pack is provisional: 123 questions are unanswered, so every figure may change before a final version.
The 4 further obligation-area rows not shown in the report need checking before printing.
Whether the University processes children's personal data, and whether any Fourth Schedule exemption for educational institutions applies, is not yet assessed; counsel to confirm.
The basis for 'Not applicable' on Significant Data Fiduciary duties should be checked against whether any Government notification exists.
The report gives no pace data for finishing critical and high work, so no completion date can be stated.
Owners and target dates for the 4 outstanding remediation actions are not in the report.
